stimulus.text:
| Law | Year | Quota rule |
| Emergency Quota Act | 1921 | 3 percent of each nationality living in the United States in 1910 |
| National Origins Act | 1924 | 2 percent of each nationality living in the United States in 1890; total cap of 150,000; immigration from Asia barred |
Neither act limited immigration from countries in the Americas.

stem: Under the 1924 act, which group faced the tightest limits on immigration?

options.text: immigrants from southern and eastern Europe
immigrants from northern and western Europe
options.misconception: The 1890 census counted many northern and western Europeans. Their quotas were the largest, not the tightest.

options.text: immigrants from Canada and from Mexico
options.misconception: The acts set no limits on immigration from countries in the Americas. Canadians and Mexicans faced no quota at all.

options.text: immigrants with family in the United States
options.misconception: Family ties did not set the quota. The law sorted people by national origin, not by family.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the 1924 act set each quota at 2 percent of that nationality in 1890, before the newer waves arrived. Southern and eastern Europeans counted least, so their quotas were smallest.
rationales.B: The 1890 census counted many northern and western Europeans. Their quotas were the largest, not the tightest.
rationales.C: The acts set no limits on immigration from countries in the Americas. Canadians and Mexicans faced no quota at all.
rationales.D: Family ties did not set the quota. The law sorted people by national origin, not by family.
rationales.general:
1. Read the 1924 rule: 2 percent of each nationality counted in 1890.
2. Ask who was scarce in 1890. Background: southern and eastern Europeans arrived mostly after 1890, so few were counted.
3. Ask what a small 1890 count means: a small quota in 1924.
4. Name the group: southern and eastern Europeans faced the tightest limits.
Remember: a quota built on an old census favors whoever arrived early.
